strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: node classification with extremely scarce minority-class labels. Retrieving existing unlabeled nodes avoids synthesizing node features and edges and provides a practical alternative to graph oversampling.

The evaluation spans five datasets, three GNN architectures, multiple imbalance ratios, and naturally imbalanced settings, with five repetitions and reported standard errors. Several gains are substantial: on CiteSeer with GCN at imbalance ratio 10, F1 improves from the best baseline's 56.32 to 64.94.

The pseudo-label diagnostics provide useful evidence about minority-class error amplification and the potential value of combining classifier predictions with embedding geometry. The appendix includes component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and substantial training and dataset details.
weaknesses: The contribution is insufficiently distinguished from its closest predecessor. Section 6 explicitly describes M3S as filtering pseudo-labels through agreement with clustering assignments, closely matching DPAM, but provides no experimental comparison. Comparisons with M3S and equally tuned class-balanced self-training are essential to establish the additional contribution.

The mathematical specification contains a consequential inconsistency. Equation 5 measures distance to the assigned class center, whereas Section 4.3 assumes this is necessarily the nearest class center. Assignment through a cluster center in Equation 4 does not guarantee that property for individual nodes. Equation 7 also needs an explicit definition of how ordered node lists become aligned numerical ranks before combination.

Evidence for the additional ranking and filtering mechanisms is mixed. In Table 11, the full method improves over geometric ranking alone by only 0.59 F1 on Cora and 0.06 on PubMed; removing DGIN improves CiteSeer F1 from 57.51 to 58.71. These results do not support uniformly beneficial components. A fixed-weight ranking combination would also help establish whether RBO-based weighting is necessary.

Reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence in the supporting experiments. In Table 8, GCN at imbalance ratio 5 reports 11,593.6 aligned and 2,308.4 discarded nodes, totaling 13,902 despite only 13,632 unlabeled nodes. Claims of consistent superiority also contradict Tables 2 and 6: UNREAL loses on Computers-Random with GraphSAGE and on Flickr balanced accuracy with GAT. These discrepancies require correction and verification.

The imbalance-trend experiments change more than imbalance alone. Ratios 20, 50, and 100 retain one minority label per class while increasing majority labels, and the citation datasets switch training-split construction at the larger ratios. This supports comparisons within each setting but weakens causal claims about degradation as imbalance increases.

Computational and reproduction details remain incomplete. Appendix D permits 40–100 training rounds with up to 2,000 epochs per later round, but provides no end-to-end runtime or measured memory comparison. Selected configurations, precise class-selection rules, and executable code are not supplied. Together with the missing closest-method comparison and unresolved reporting errors, these gaps outweigh the promising reported gains.
